Shittah
SHIT-tah
n. (the acacia tree of the desert; source of shittim wood)
Hebrew shittah, the acacia; its plural shittim gives the familiar shittim wood of the tabernacle. The acacia is the one substantial timber of the Sinai wilderness — hard, close-grained, thorny, and resistant to decay and insects.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together. Isaiah is promising that God will make a forest where there is sand, and the shittah stands in the list as the one tree that already belongs there. That is what makes it significant. The acacia is the desert's own timber, thorny and unlovely, and it is the wood God specified for the furniture of his dwelling: they shall make an ark of shittim wood; and, thou shalt make boards for the tabernacle of shittim wood standing up. The ark of the covenant, the table, the altar, and the frame of the tent itself were all built from the only tree the wilderness had. God did not import cedar from Lebanon for the tabernacle. He took what grew where his people were, hard and incorruptible and full of thorns, and overlaid it with gold. The pattern is worth naming plainly, because Scripture uses it everywhere: God takes what the wilderness produces and makes it the place of his presence. Isaiah's promise then adds the purpose, and it is not horticultural — that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), under SHITTAH and SHITTIM: a species of tree, and the wood of it, used in the construction of the Jewish tabernacle; supposed to be a species of acacia.

expand to see more

SHITTAH, SHITTIM, n. A sort of precious wood, of which the tables, altars and boards of the Jewish tabernacle were made.

ACACIA, n. A genus of plants, chiefly natives of warm climates, many of them thorny.

MYRTLE, n. A plant or shrub of the genus Myrtus, an evergreen with fragrant leaves.

WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.

INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot corrupt or decay; not admitting of corruption.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 41:19 — "I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:"

Isaiah 41:20 — "That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it."

Exodus 25:10 — "And they shall make an ark of shittim wood: two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof."

Exodus 26:15 — "And thou shalt make boards for the tabernacle of shittim wood standing up."

Modern Corruption

Tabernacle materials are treated either as incidental practicalities or as a code in which every detail is decoded into a doctrine; Scripture gives them as chosen and specified by God, with meaning the text itself supplies.

expand to see more

The first reduction treats shittim wood as a matter of availability — the Israelites used acacia because acacia was what grew in Sinai — and so drains the specification of significance. Availability is real, and the dictionary does not dispute it. But the text does not present the materials as improvisation; it presents them as commanded, in extraordinary detail, according to a pattern shewed in the mount. That God's chosen material was the wilderness's own thorn tree is the sort of thing Scripture does on purpose, and the whole letter to the Hebrews is built on the assumption that the tabernacle's details were meant to teach.

The opposite excess turns every board and pin into an allegory, so that the acacia's incorruptibility becomes a proof text for the impeccability of Christ's human nature and each measurement yields a doctrine. Typology is legitimate and the New Testament practises it; the discipline is to follow where the apostles actually go and to hold the rest with an open hand. The safe ground here is what Isaiah states: God plants trees in a desert, and he does it that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand that his hand has done it. The wood points to the Builder.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shittah (H7848), the acacia tree; midbar (H4057), wilderness; aron (H727), ark or chest; hadas (H1918), myrtle.

expand to see more

Hebrew shittah (H7848) — the acacia; rendered shittah tree here and shittim wood in Exodus.

Hebrew midbar (H4057) — wilderness, uninhabited pasture; where God promises to plant a forest.

Hebrew aron (H727) — a chest or ark; the ark of the covenant, made of this wood.

Hebrew hadas (H1918) — myrtle; named with the shittah in Isaiah's planting.

Hebrew bara (H1254) — to create; the Holy One of Israel hath created it.

Usage

"“the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle” — a forest promised in the desert."

"“an ark of shittim wood” — the wilderness tree in the holiest place."

"“that they may see, and know, and consider” — the stated purpose."
